title: Contextualized Evaluation of Vision Language Models through Dynamic Interviews
claim: Prior evaluation uses static one-shot probes; ours runs a dynamic, multi-turn, context-aware interaction among examinee, examiner, and grader.
layout: 3 regions: roles diagram left, static baselines middle, dynamic dialogue right
description: The left region shows a triangle of three roles: the examinee (a blue robot, with OpenAI, Gemini, Qwen and Claude logos in a box), the grader, and the examiner. Arrows labeled 'grade' and 'question' connect them. Two callout boxes list the grader's methods (CHAIR, LLM judge, tool call, scene graph) and the examiner's options (caption-based, Yes/No Q&A, dynamic Q&A). The right region contrasts prior static examiners with CEDI. Caption-based examiners are shown as a single prompt with one long description. Single-turn Yes/No (POPE) is shown as stacked short questions with a 'Yes / No' answer. The CEDI column shows a multi-turn chat. Green question bubbles alternate with blue answer bubbles, and red highlighted words mark a premise rejection and a refusal. The eye goes first to the colorful robot triangle, then to the chat on the right.
caption: CEDI's three-party interaction (left) contrasted with prior static examiners (right).
abstract: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial advances on benchmarks, yet their real-world effectiveness remains uncertain. This gap stems from the fundamental misalignment between benchmarks in controlled, static settings and the dynamic, interactive, and contextualized nature of real-world applications. To bridge this gap, we propose CEDI (Contextualized Evaluation of MLLMs through Dynamic, multi-round Interactions, a framework that recasts evaluation as a three-party interaction between an evaluatee model, an automated examiner, and a grader. The examiner conducts multi-turn, semi-structured conversations guided by a graph-based representation of the task. By navigating state-space transitions, CEDI deploys diverse strategies, from clarification requests to adversarial probes, to elicit performance evidence. We apply CEDI to visual hallucinations. Empirical results across multiple models, diverse settings, datasets, and domains show that contextualized, interactive evaluations reveal not only significantly more hallucinations than conventional static evaluation but also ones that more closely resemble those arising in practical use cases. We further show that hallucinations often accumulate over long contexts, through self-reinforcing dialogue history, and models are particularly vulnerable to questions requiring premise rejection or refusal. Together, these findings highlight CEDI as a step toward realistic, systematic, and ecologically valid assessments of MLLMs' capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/williamium3000/cedi.
